content: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a type of pneumonia that occurs in patients who have been on mechanical ventilation for at least 48 hours. It is a serious complication in critically ill patients. Oral hygiene care (OHC), which involves the use of mouthrinses, gels, swabs, toothbrushes, or combinations of these, along with suctioning of secretions, may help reduce the risk of VAP in these patients. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of oral hygiene care on the incidence of VAP in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation in intensive care units (ICUs). To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including Cochrane Oral Health’s Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and CINAHL, up to February 25, 2020. Additional searches were performed in the VIP Database, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for ongoing trials. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the effects of oral hygiene care in mechanically ventilated patients. Data from these trials were independently reviewed, extracted, and analyzed by at least two authors. Risk ratios (RR) and mean differences (MD) were calculated using a random-effects model for meta-analysis when data from four or more trials were available. A total of 40 RCTs involving 5,675 participants from various countries, including China, the USA, Brazil, and Iran, were included. These trials were categorized into five main comparisons: 1. Chlorhexidine (CHX) mouthrinse or gel versus placebo or usual care. 2. CHX mouthrinse versus other oral care agents. 3. Toothbrushing (with or without antiseptics) versus no toothbrushing (with or without antiseptics). 4. Powered versus manual toothbrushing. 5. Comparisons of other oral care agents (either versus placebo/usual care or head-to-head comparisons). The overall risk of bias was assessed as high in 31 trials, low in two trials, and unclear in the remaining trials. Moderate-certainty evidence from 13 RCTs (1,206 participants, 92% adults) indicated that CHX mouthrinse or gel, as part of oral hygiene care, likely reduces the incidence of VAP compared to placebo or usual care. The incidence of VAP decreased from 26% to approximately 18% (RR 0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47 to 0.97; P = 0.03; I² = 66%). This corresponds to a number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) of 12, meaning that providing oral hygiene care with CHX to 12 ventilated patients in the ICU would prevent one case of VAP. There was no evidence of a difference between interventions for mortality (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.33; P = 0.86; I² = 0%; 9 RCTs, 944 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), duration of mechanical ventilation (MD -1.10 days, 95% CI -3.20 to 1.00 days; P = 0.30; I² = 74%; 4 RCTs, 594 participants; very low-certainty evidence), or duration of ICU stay (MD -0.89 days, 95% CI -3.59 to 1.82 days; P = 0.52; I² = 69%; 5 RCTs, 627 participants; low-certainty evidence). Adverse effects were rarely reported. One study noted mild adverse effects with similar frequency in both CHX and control groups, while another study reported no adverse effects. Toothbrushing (with or without antiseptics) may reduce the incidence of VAP compared to oral hygiene care without toothbrushing (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.91; P = 0.01; I² = 40%; 5 RCTs, 910 participants; low-certainty evidence). There is also some evidence suggesting that toothbrushing may reduce the duration of ICU stay (MD -1.89 days, 95% CI -3.52 to -0.27 days; P = 0.02; I² = 0%; 3 RCTs, 749 participants), but this evidence is of very low certainty. Low-certainty evidence did not show a reduction in mortality (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.05; P = 0.12; I² = 0%; 5 RCTs, 910 participants) or duration of mechanical ventilation (MD -0.43 days, 95% CI -1.17 to 0.30 days; P = 0.25; I² = 46%; 4 RCTs, 810 participants). In conclusion, the use of chlorhexidine mouthwash or gel as part of oral hygiene care likely reduces the incidence of VAP in critically ill patients from 26% to approximately 18% compared to placebo or usual care. However, there was no evidence of a difference in mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, or ICU stay. Oral hygiene care that includes both antiseptics and toothbrushing may be more effective than antiseptics alone in reducing the incidence of VAP and ICU stay, but the evidence is of low certainty. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether any of the interventions are associated with adverse effects.
